title: Queen Chudala asks, who am I?
hookLine: a queen finds freedom at home, and her husband laughs
carry: the atman is found within, not far away
tomorrow: the queen follows him to the forest, in disguise. why?
last: A SMALL ROOM CAN HOLD A WORLD.

lines: THE REAL YOU IS FAR AWAY?
cards: Find yourself on a beach. Find yourself on a mountain. Travel ads love that line: the real you is somewhere far away.
Vasistha tells Rama a story that turns it around. Queen Chudala changes. She's calm in a way her husband, King Shikhidhvaja, isn't; she seems lit from inside.
He asks her what happened. She tells him, plainly. And he laughs.
Why would the one who understands be the one nobody believes?

teach.b: Here's how she got there. Chudala asked herself one question: who am I?
Not this body, she saw. Not the senses. Not even the restless mind.
Underneath them all she found the Self, the atman, which Hindu teaching holds is your truest nature, the awareness that knows them.
And resting there, she became free, right where she was: a wife and a queen, in a palace. That's the puzzle of the laugh.

teach.h: THE KING GOES TO THE FOREST.
teach.b: The king hears pretty words from a woman who has never left her comforts. Freedom, he's sure, is found by giving things up, somewhere far from here. So he grows restless and leaves for the forest to live as an ascetic.
Chudala tries to talk him out of it, then lets him go, and rules the kingdom while he's away.
Hindus call her way self-inquiry, and it is still taught: in the last century the sage Ramana Maharshi gave seekers the same question, who am I?

In the story, the one who is truly free never leaves home. The one who walks away to find freedom hasn't found it yet. And a question hangs over the forest: will the king ever learn what his wife already knows?

how: Readers of the Yoga Vasistha often single out Chudala as a woman teacher of freedom; her story is retold in talks and books on Vedanta.

o: a sage's story of a queen who finds freedom at home
a story of a king who teaches his wife to meditate
a story of a queen who leaves her palace for the woods

games.q: the queen and the king — tap the pairs.
p: the king who laughs, then leaves
the Self: the awareness that knows

s: in the story, the king becomes free first and teaches his wife
Chudala is free first, at home; he doesn't believe her.
Chudala finds freedom by asking 'who am I?'
not the body, not the senses, not the mind, but the Self that knows them.
the story says freedom requires leaving home for the forest
Chudala finds it in the palace; the king goes to the forest still looking.

games.q: a friend quits her job to find peace on a long trip, and tells you peace can't be found where you live. what does Chudala's story say?
o: peace isn't a place; it can be found right at home.
she's right; peace only comes far from ordinary life.
trips are a waste; staying home is the only way.
games.why: Chudala becomes free in the palace by asking who am I. the story doesn't forbid the forest; it says the finding isn't a place.

practice: Close your eyes if you're comfortable. Notice the body sitting: that's known. Notice a sound or a sensation: that's known too.
Notice a thought passing: known. For the rest of the time, rest as the one who notices, without chasing any of it.

wordCard.voice: The Yoga Vasistha: here, Queen Chudala, free at home by asking who am I, and a husband who doesn't believe her.

orig.note: Sanskrit atman: the Self, the awareness Chudala finds beneath body, senses and mind.

carryVoice: Carry this: the atman is found within, not far away. Chudala found it at home. That's sixteen-oh-five.
